[MUQATIL:2:185/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The Quran came down from the Preserved Tablet over twenty months, and Gabriel brought it down over twenty years.
[MUQATIL:2:185/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The Quran guides in religion and gives clear proofs that distinguish guidance from doubt and misguidance; Muqatil glosses the criterion in 3:4 as an exit from doubts. | mentions 3:4
[MUQATIL:2:185/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Anyone present for Ramadan must fast and not eat.
[MUQATIL:2:185/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | A sick person who breaks the fast makes up the same number of days after recovery; the traveler does likewise, continuously or on separate days as desired.
[MUQATIL:2:185/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Ease means gentleness in religious duties through the concession allowing the sick and traveler to break the fast; without it, the duty would be hardship.
[MUQATIL:2:185/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Completing the count means making up the full number of counted days; takbir means magnifying God for His guidance in religion, and the verse calls people to thank Him for that blessing.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]هذانرجلانوعبداللهمنطلقين|وإنمانصبتالمنطلقين#234/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The accusative منطلقين is a circumstantial predicate: it cannot modify only عبدالله or both the two men and عبدالله as an adjective.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]هذانرجلانوعبداللهمنطلقين|وإنمانصبتالمنطلقين#234/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The nominative dual منطلقان is also possible when the predicate is understood to describe only the two men, excluding عبدالله.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]هذانرجلانوعبداللهمنطلقين|وإنمانصبتالمنطلقين#234/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With هؤلاء ناس and عبدالله, accusative منطلقين makes a shared circumstantial phrase; nominative منطلقون instead agrees with ناس alone.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]هذانرجلانوعبداللهمنطلقين|وإنمانصبتالمنطلقين#234/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The sheep-and-lamb example means one dirham for each sheep and its lamb; in this construction the lamb is not included in كل as a definite item.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]هذانرجلانوعبداللهمنطلقين|وإنمانصبتالمنطلقين#234/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | Sībawayh prefers راتعين with كل شاة وسخلتها and وهذه ناقة وفصيلها: it is more common and analogical; some Arabs use the alternative nominative.
[AKHFASH:v1p169#2/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | ولتكملوا continues the preceding clause with an understood يريد: God wants you to complete the count and magnify Him.
[AKHFASH:v1p169#2/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | يريد الله ليبين لكم means He wants this in order to explain to you; alternatively, an omitted أن after the lām governs the verb, as in 2:213. | mentions 2:213
[AKHFASH:v1p169#2/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The poem أريد لأنسى likewise means I want this thing in order to forget her, with the intended object of يريد left implicit.
[AKHFASH:v1p169#2/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | شهر رمضان explains the previously mentioned counted days: those days are the month of Ramadan. | mentions 2:184
[AKHFASH:v1p169#2/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · بعضهم | reports | Some read شهر رمضان in the accusative, either as an imperative understood as 'Ramadan, so fast,' or as a time adverbial to the fasting obligation; رمضان is genitive by annexation and diptote.
[AKHFASH:v1p169#2/r6] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | هدى and بينات are accusative because the verb is already occupied by القرآن, like وجد عبد الله ظريفا.
[AKHFASH:v1p169#2/r7] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | الفرقان is genitive, coordinated with the من in من الفرقان.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p73#4/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The earlier provision allowing a ransom meal for one poor person was abrogated by the command to fast when present for the month. | mentions 2:185
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p73#4/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Al-shahr is accusative as a temporal adverb, not as an object of shahida; the sense is whoever is present during the month and is not traveling should fast.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p73#4/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Being present during the month can describe either a resident or a traveler, which is why shahida is not construed as taking the month as its object.
[TAB-FULL:v3p187#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī derives shahr from public appearance: a sword is made visible when drawn, the new moon appears, and one enters a month when it begins.
[TAB-FULL:v3p187#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض أهل المعرفة بلغة العرب | reports | An Arab-language authority says Ramaḍān was named for intense heat, when young camels' feet were scorched, as other months were named for seasons or pilgrimage.
[TAB-FULL:v3p187#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid disliked saying Ramaḍān alone, suspecting it may be one of God's names, and preferred the Qurʾānic phrase “month of Ramaḍān.”
[TAB-FULL:v3p187#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The nominative shahr can explain the counted days in 2:184, or mean “that is Ramaḍān” or “Ramaḍān is prescribed for you.” | mentions 2:184
[TAB-FULL:v3p187#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض القراء | reports | Some reciters read shahr in the accusative, construed as the object of prescribed fasting, the month to be fasted, an imperative to fast it, or a time expression meaning fasting during Ramaḍān. | mentions 2:184
[TAB-FULL:v3p187#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The Qurʾān descended from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr in Ramaḍān, then came to Muḥammad in stages as God willed.
[TAB-FULL:v3p187#2/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the Qurʾān descended all at once from al-Dhikr to the House of Might on the twenty-fourth night of Ramaḍān; al-Suddī also gives this account.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbī says it had reached him that the Qurʾān descended all at once to the lowest heaven.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the Qurʾān descended all at once to Gabriel on Laylat al-Qadr and Gabriel brought it to Muḥammad only when commanded. | mentions 97:1, 44:3
[TAB-FULL:v3p192#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj explains that each year's revelations came on Laylat al-Qadr from the seventh heaven to Gabriel in the lowest heaven, and Gabriel delivered them only on his Lord's command. | mentions 97:1, 44:3
[TAB-FULL:v3p192#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Answering a doubt about the three verses naming a Ramadan night despite revelations in other months, Ibn ʿAbbās says the Qurʾān descended together that night and then piecemeal on its occasions. | mentions 44:3, 97:1
[TAB-FULL:v3p192#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The Qurʾān is guidance for people toward the path of truth and the right course.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Its clear proofs explain God's limits, obligations, lawful matters, and prohibitions.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192#2/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-furqān means the distinction between truth and falsehood.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192#2/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī glosses the clear proofs of guidance and criterion as proofs about the lawful and unlawful.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd b. Jubayr says the Qurʾān descended all at once on Laylat al-Qadr in Ramaḍān and was placed in the lowest heaven.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from the Prophet dates the scriptures' descents: Abraham's on the first night of Ramaḍān, Torah on the sixth, Gospel on the thirteenth, and Qurʾān on the twenty-fourth.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by al-Suddī, identifies Laylat al-Qadr with the blessed night: the Qurʾān descended together to al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr in the lowest heaven, then reached Muḥammad gradually in commands, prohibitions, and battles.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says God sent the Qurʾān to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr, then sent portions when He willed, linking this to 97:1. | mentions 97:1
[TAB-FULL:v3p192/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Another wording of Ibn ʿAbbās's account adds that twenty years elapsed between the Qurʾān's first and last revelation.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the whole Qurʾān descended to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr, then came down from it as God brought events to pass until it was gathered.
[TAB-FULL:v3p192/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the Qurʾān descended together from the highest heaven to the lowest on Laylat al-Qadr and was then distributed over the years, citing 56:75. | mentions 56:75
[TAB-FULL:v3p193/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains witnessing the month as Ramadan beginning while one is resident at home, which obligates fasting.
[TAB-FULL:v3p193/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | A second report from Ibn Abbas says that one who meets Ramadan resident must fast even if he travels, while one meeting it already traveling may fast or break.
[TAB-FULL:v3p193/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبيدة | reports | Ubayda says that a man who reaches Ramadan resident must fast its remainder even if he travels.
[TAB-FULL:v3p193/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبيدة | reports | Asked about a man who reaches Ramadan while resident, Ubayda says fasting its beginning obligates fasting its end.
[TAB-FULL:v3p193/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says whoever enters Ramadan at home must fast, and must keep fasting if he leaves because Ramadan began while he was home.
[TAB-FULL:v3p193/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · علي | reports | A report tentatively attributed to Ali says one who is resident when Ramadan ar

[TAB-FULL:v3p195/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبيدة | reports | Ubayda says whoever witnesses the beginning of Ramadan should fast through its end.

[TAB-FULL:v3p195/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · آخرون | reports | Another interpretation takes witnessing the month to mean fasting only the portion of it one actually witnesses.

[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r10] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | In the Hanafi account, one who enters Ramadan sane but becomes insane and recovers after the month must make up the days lost to insanity.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r11] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | They also require someone who entered Ramadan insane but recovered before its end to make up the month except the day after recovery.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r12] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | They say no make-up is due if someone remains insane for the entire month and recovers only after it ends.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبوه | reports | Saʿd’s son reports that Ali fasted while returning to Medina from his estate, while his walking companion broke his fast.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبوه | reports | A second report from Ali’s companion says Ali fasted on the return journey and ordered the companion, who was walking, to break his fast.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi reports that he traveled in Ramadan and broke his fast at the bridge.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · سفيان | reports | Sufyan says he prefers completing the Ramadan fast while traveling.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحكم وحماد | reports | Al-Hakam and Hammad tell al-Ashʿath to go ahead with his planned Ramadan journey.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · إبراهيم | reports | Hammad reports Ibrahim’s preference that a traveler remain in place during Ramadan’s last ten days.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن وسعيد بن المسيب | reports | Al-Hasan and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib say someone who begins Ramadan resident and then travels may choose whether to break the fast.
[TAB-FULL:v3p197/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | Abu Hanifa and his companions interpret witnessing the month as being sane, adult, and legally obligated to fast.
[TAB-FULL:v3p200/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Al-Tabari rejects defining witnessing as legal competence: if insanity excuses a whole month, the same logic would excuse other total loss of reason, yet consensus requires make-up after unconsciousness or brain fever.
[TAB-FULL:v3p200/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet traveled from Medina to Mecca in Ramadan and publicly drank at Asfan.
[TAB-FULL:v3p200/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that in the conquest year the Prophet fasted after leaving, then broke his fast at al-Kadid; reports vary whether he left after ten or twenty days.
[TAB-FULL:v3p200/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | Abu Saʿid reports that during a Ramadan journey with the Prophet some companions fasted and others broke their fast, without mutual criticism.
[TAB-FULL:v3p200/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Tabari rejects both the adult-capacity and resident-at-month-start readings, preferring that residents fast the days they witness and sick or traveling people make up missed days.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | A sick person or traveler who breaks the fast during Ramadan must make up exactly the days missed on other days outside Ramadan.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r10] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari explains أخر as the plural of أخرى, following the same pattern as الكبرى and القربى.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · إبراهيم | reports | Ibrahim’s reported threshold for breaking the fast is illness that prevents a person from standing for prayer.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · إبراهيم | reports | A second report from Ibrahim likewise permits a sick person to break the fast if he cannot pray standing.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says a fasting person may break when fasting overwhelms him and prevents him from performing obligatory prayers as prescribed.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · محمد بن إدريس الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi allows breaking for any illness that fasting would likely worsen beyond what the person can bear.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · آخرون | reports | Another view permits breaking for any condition that is called an illness.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · محمد بن سيرين | reports | A report illustrates the broad illness view: Ibn Sirin was eating in Ramadan and afterward explained that his finger hurt.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Tabari prefers allowing the fast to be broken when it causes intolerable hardship; otherwise a person who can fast must fulfill the obligation.
[TAB-FULL:v3p202/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The phrase “a number of other days” means counted days other than the days of Ramadan. | mentions 2:184
[TAB-FULL:v3p204/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Although اليوم is masculine, plural الأيام is treated as feminine, so أخر agrees with the plural; Arabic does not say أجمعون for الأيام or أيام آخرون.
[TAB-FULL:v3p204/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari raises whether an excused sick person or traveler who fasts Ramadan has fulfilled the obligation, whether make-up remains due, and whether fasting Ramadan is permitted for them. | mentions 2:184
[TAB-FULL:v3p204/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · آخرون | reports | One view treats breaking the fast during illness or travel as a binding divine command, not a mere concession.
[TAB-FULL:v3p204/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas calls breaking the fast while traveling a binding obligation.
[TAB-FULL:v3p204/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar likens the travel concession to charity from God: refusing a charity offered to someone would provoke anger.
[TAB-FULL:v3p204/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abu Jaʿfar says his father did not fast while traveling and used to forbid it.
[TAB-FULL:v3p204/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak disliked fasting while traveling.
[TAB-FULL:v3p204/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أهل هذه المقالة | reports | Those who treat breaking as obligatory say that a traveler who fasts must make up the fast after returning.
[TAB-FULL:v3p207/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عمر | reports | Two reports say Umar ordered a man who fasted while traveling to repeat the fast.
[TAB-FULL:v3p207/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abu Hurayra tells his son, who fasted while he broke the fast during Ramadan travel, that he must make it up after settling.
[TAB-FULL:v3p207/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عروة | reports | Urwa is reported to have ordered a man who fasted while traveling to make up the fast.
[TAB-FULL:v3p207/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | When travelers told Umar ibn al-Khattab they had fasted, he asked whether they could bear it and repeatedly ordered them to make up the fast.
[TAB-FULL:v3p207/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أهل هذه المقالة | reports | Their argument is that residents are commanded to fast Ramadan, whereas the sick and traveler are assigned an equal number of later days; therefore a traveler may not substitute a Ramadan fast.
[TAB-FULL:v3p208/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A hadith attributed to the Prophet says that one who fasts while traveling is like one who does not fast while resident.
[TAB-FULL:v3p208/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · آخرون | reports | Another view treats travel fasting as the continuing obligation and breaking as a divine concession; fasting in travel needs no make-up.

[TAB-FULL:v3p208/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | A report says Umar fasted during a Ramadan journey, then continued fasting with the people when the month’s status on the return journey raised concern about br

item.text: The early sources already show several recurring disputes: how the Qur’an’s descent in Ramadan is understood, what it means to “witness” the month, when illness or travel permits a missed fast, and whether a traveler’s fast counts. I’m tracking the smaller grammatical, reading, and report details alongside those.

[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p201#2/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that at Ramadan the devils are chained, the gates of Paradise opened, and the gates of Hell closed.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p201#2/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A second Abū Hurayra report says that on Ramadan’s first night devils and rebellious jinn are chained, Hell’s gates shut, Paradise’s gates open, a caller summons good and restrains evil, and people are freed from the Fire nightly.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p201#2/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that whoever fasts Ramadan, prays during it, or stands on Laylat al-Qadr in faith and expectation of reward is forgiven past sins.

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p252#3/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Ramadan derives from رمض, to burn, associated with the heat of the hot ground; the month is attached to the word and the name is made proper.

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p252#3/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | A reading in the accusative construes شهر رمضان as an imperative to fast, a substitute for أيام معدودات, or the object of أن تصوموا in 2:184. | mentions 2:184
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p252#3/r8] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The Qur'an's descent in Ramadan means its revelation began then, on Laylat al-Qadr.

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p254#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Completing the count is the purpose of keeping track of missed days; magnifying God is the purpose of the prescribed way of making them up; gratitude is the purpose of the concession and ease.

[TABRISI:2:185#5/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | In the report's continuation, Abraham's scriptures are dated to the first or third night of Ramadan; Moses' Torah to the sixth, Jesus' Gospel to the thirteenth, David's Psalms to the eighteenth, and the Qur'an to the twenty-fourth. Al-ʿAyyāshī transmits this from al-Ṣādiq and his forefathers, ending with the Prophet.
[TABRISI:2:185#5/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another interpretation takes أنزل فيه القرآن to mean that the Qur'an was revealed concerning the obligation and prescription of fasting, with فيه meaning concerning its prescription.
[TABRISI:2:185#5/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The Qur'an is guidance for people, directing them to the kinds of knowledge they are obligated to acquire, and its signs are proofs of guidance.
[TABRISI:2:185#5/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the first guidance is guidance away from error, while the second means clarification of the lawful and unlawful.
[TABRISI:2:185#5/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · الأصم | reports | Al-Aṣamm and al-Qāḍī say the first guidance is the initial knowledge required of people; the second comprises accounts of prophets, their laws, and histories, which are known through the Qur'an.
[TABRISI:2:185#6/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Furqān is that which separates truth from falsehood.
[TABRISI:2:185#6/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Abū ʿAbd Allāh distinguishes the Qur'an as the book as a whole from the Furqān, the decisive rulings that must be followed.
[TABRISI:2:185#6/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | In a sermon reported by al-Bāqir through al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, Abū Ayyūb, and Abū al-Ward, the Prophet describes Ramadan's night better than a thousand months, obligatory fast, and voluntary night prayer worth seventy months' prayers; good deeds equal obligatory deeds elsewhere and an obligatory deed equals seventy. He calls it a month of patience, mutual aid, and increased provision; feeding a faster brings emancipation and forgiveness, even a sip of milk, water, or a few dates suffices, and easing a servant's work eases one's reckoning. He describes its beginning as mercy, middle as forgiveness, and end as answered prayer and release from fire; he urges testimony, asking for needs and Paradise, and seeking refuge from Hell.
[TABRISI:2:185#6/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · سلمان الفارسي | reports | Salman al-Fārisī's version urges four practices: the testimony of faith and seeking forgiveness please God, while asking for Paradise and refuge from Hell are indispensable.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | The Prophet is reported to say that a fasting person's sleep is worship, silence is glorification, prayer is answered, and deeds are multiplied.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan and others require making up missed days immediately once the sick person recovers or the traveler returns.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa allows make-up days to be delayed; the Imāmī school sets the period before the next Ramadan, allows consecutive or separate days, and prefers consecutive days.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | If make-up fasting is delayed until another Ramadan arrives, fidya is due along with the make-up fast; al-Shāfiʿī agrees.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God wills ease by granting the sick and traveler a dispensation not to fast during those circumstances.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another interpretation takes God's willing ease to apply to all human affairs.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | rejects | Tabrisi uses the verse against the compulsion doctrine: God wills ease in some human acts, does not will hardship in others, and therefore does not will imposing the impossible.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | prefers | The stronger reading is that one who is present in town and not away during Ramadan must fast the whole month; الشهر is definite for the known month.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو جعفر | reports | Asked about the wording, Abū Jaʿfar says it plainly means whoever witnesses Ramadan should fast it, while whoever travels in it should break the fast; this report is from Zurāra.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · علي | reports | ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and other exegetes say that entering Ramadan while resident obliges fasting its entire month.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | A second reading takes the phrase to mean a legally responsible person who is resident when the month arrives must fast that month; it abrogates the earlier choice of fasting or fidya, since recitation order does not determine order of revelation. Tabrisi prefers the first reading.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The qualifying illness is one that makes a person fear an extreme worsening of the illness.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Abū Baṣīr reports that al-Ṣādiq leaves assessment of illness to the person: if weak, break the fast; if strong enough, fast, whatever the illness.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن | reports | Another transmitted definition is any illness that prevents someone from standing for as long as a prayer; al-Ḥasan holds this, and jurists disagree.
[TABRISI:2:185#7/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | In the Imāmī school, a journey allowing a fast to be broken is permitted or devotional and measures eight farsakhs, twenty-four miles; al-Shāfiʿī requires sixteen farsakhs and Abū Ḥanīfa twenty-four.
[TABRISI:2:185#8/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The completion is the make-up of the days missed through illness or travel, fasted after recovery or return; alternatively, the concession to break the fast was prescribed so the count could be completed later.
[TABRISI:2:185#8/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another possibility is completing the month's count: people without an excuse complete it then, while the sick and travelers complete it at another time.
[TABRISI:2:185#8/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | rejects | Those who argue Ramadan is never shorter say the command requires an undiminished full count; Tabrisi answers that the required count may be twenty-nine or thirty days, or that

[TABRISI:2:185#8/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | In the Imāmī school, this refers to the takbīr on the night of Eid al-Fiṭr after Maghrib, ʿIshāʾ, dawn, and the Eid prayer.
[TABRISI:2:185#8/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and others interpret it as saying the takbīr on Eid day.
[TABRISI:2:185#8/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another interpretation is to magnify God for guiding people to the religious laws.
[TABRISI:2:185#8/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The verse's close means that people should thank God for His blessings.
[TABRISI:2:185/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Al-ʿAyyāshī transmits from Muḥammad ibn Muslim that the Prophet first broke a Ramadan journey fast at Kurāʿ al-Ghamīm, ordered the people to break theirs, and called those who continued disobedient; the name persisted until his death.
[TABRISI:2:185/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Shaʿbī understand the phrase to cover all people under an initial choice between fasting and feeding, later abrogated by the command to fast when present for Ramadan.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p386/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | In ordinary Arabic ṣawm is abstention in general; horses are called fasting when they stop moving, and wind when it stops blowing.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p386/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The cited line’s word ṣiyām describes horses that refrain from moving beneath the dust and chew their reins.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p386/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | In religious law fasting is abstaining from food, drink, and sex together with the intention.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p386/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | One Qur’anic sense of ṣawm is the legally prescribed fast.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p459#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Furqān derives from tafrīq; farq is the splitting open of a thing.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p459#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | Furqān can mean a way out in religion from error and doubt. | mentions 3:4, 8:29
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Whoever witnesses the month means whoever is resident and not traveling.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The Sunna is to proclaim takbīr on the nights of Eid al-Fiṭr and Eid al-Aḍḥā and while going to the prayer ground.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · حنبل عن أحمد | reports | In one report from Aḥmad, the takbīr for Eid al-Fiṭr ends after the imam finishes the sermon.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الأثرم عن أحمد | reports | Another report from Aḥmad says it ends upon reaching the prayer ground; al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā explains this as reaching the ground when the imam comes out.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The sickness and travel exemption is repeated because the earlier verse included an abrogated ruling; repeating it prevents the exemption from being attached to that abrogated material. | mentions 2:184
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة والضحاك | reports | They interpret ease as breaking the fast while traveling and hardship as fasting during travel.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz says to choose whichever is easier for oneself, fasting or breaking the fast on a journey.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي وأبو بكر عن عاصم | reports | Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read the kāf lightly; Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim reads the mīm doubled, like waṣṣā and awṣā.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says this means completing the number of days missed.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Another explanation says not to exceed what was prescribed, as Christians did, or move it from its proper time.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says Muslims should begin glorifying God upon seeing the Shawwāl crescent and continue until the end of their Eid.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187#2/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbārī says the lām clauses coordinate with an omitted lām: God wills ease, not hardship, and [wills] that people complete the count; the first lām is omitted because its sense is clear.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash reads shahr in the nominative as an explanation of the previously mentioned ‘few days’: those days are the month of Ramadan.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مجاهد ومعاوية والحسن وزيد بن علي وعكرمة ويحيى بن يعمر | reports | Mujāhid reads shahr in the accusative as an exhortation: ‘Ramadan is prescribed for you, so fast it’; Muʿāwiya, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿIkrima, and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar also read it accusatively. | mentions 22:78, 2:138
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن فارس | reports | Ibn Fāris connects Ramaḍān with intense heat of sun-heated stones; the month was named when transferred from the old calendar because it coincided with hot weather.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | One view says the whole Quran descended in Ramadan on the Night of Power to Bayt al-ʿIzza in the lowest heaven.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مجاهد والضحاك | reports | Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk explain its being sent down in Ramadan as the establishment of the fast as an obligation then.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن إسحاق وأبو سليمان الدمشقي | reports | Ibn Isḥāq and Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī say the Quran’s revelation to the Prophet began in Ramadan.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p187/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil glosses al-furqān as a way out of religious doubt and error.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p64/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazila argue that seeking refuge makes the servant the originator of actions: if God creates an act, the servant cannot perform or resist it.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p64/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | They argue that refuge is coherent only if God did not create the evil sought refuge from; otherwise the servant seeks refuge from God's own act.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p64/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | They infer that seeking refuge from sins shows the servant rejects them, whereas a person must accept what God decrees if God creates sins.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p64/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | They argue that if Satan has no role in whispering and God creates it, one should seek refuge from God rather than Satan.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p64/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشيطان | reports | In a fifth objection, Satan says that if God decrees his whispering while affirming that He wills ease and does not burden beyond capacity, condemning him conflicts with divine wisdom and mercy. | mentions 2:286, 22:78
[RAZI-FULL:v1p64/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشيطان | reports | In a sixth objection, Satan asks whether his being accursed follows a sin he committed: if so determinism fails, and if not, the punishment is unjust despite God's denial of injustice. | mentions 40:31
[RAZI-FULL:v1p64/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Rāzī rejects the proposed kasb as a middle position: if human power independently affects an act, the view is Muʿtazilī; if not, it is pure determinism and the objections still apply.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p62/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On either identification of the numbered days, some abrogation is required; if they were Ramadan, the next verse abrogates the option, though al-Razi flags a problem with treating an immediately connected verse as abrogator. | mentions 2:185
[RAZI-FULL:v5p64#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās a Prophetic rule against shortening prayer on a journey shorter than four mail-stations, from Mecca to ʿAsfān; each station is four farsakhs, totaling sixteen.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p64#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس ومالك | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly told ʿAṭāʾ that trips to ʿArafa or Mar al-Ẓahrān do not qualify, but journeys to Jeddah, ʿAsfān, or Ṭāʾif do; Mālik says Mecca to Jeddah or ʿAsfān is four stations.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p64#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa argues that the verse commands fasting; a three-day travel concession is established by consensus, while shorter journeys are disputed, so the fasting rule remains for them.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p64#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | A Prophetic report permits wiping over footwear for one day and night to a resident and three days and nights to a traveler; Abū Ḥanīfa infers a three-day minimum travel period from the ruling’s cause-and-effect relation.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p64#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Against prioritizing caution in worship, al-Razi prefers the legal aim of travel relief, supported by the Prophet’s description of the concession as God’s charity to be accepted; that specific evidence outweighs general caution.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p64#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The wiping report does not establish a three-day minimum for travel: stating a resident wipes one day does not preclude residence after an hour, and the traveler’s three-day allowance likewise does not exclude shorter travel.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p66/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أنس بن مالك وعثمان بن أبي أوفى والشافعي وأبو حنيفة ومالك والثوري وأبو يوسف ومحمد | holds | Anas, Uthman ibn Abi Awfa, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Thawri, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad hold that fasting while travelling is better.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p67/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · فرقة ثالثة | reports | The third group's view is supported by God's statement that He intends ease, so a traveller sho

[RAZI-FULL:v5p69/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Making the witnessing-Ramadan verse an abrogator would contradict the adjacent declaration that God intends ease, since this reading changes restrictive obligation to an option and reverses ease and hardship.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisa'i reads shahr in the nominative as a substitute for al-siyam: fasting prescribed for you means the month of Ramadan.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God singled Ramadan out for fasting because He singled it out for the greatest sign of lordship, the Quran's revelation; fasting is a fitting great sign of servanthood.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says fasting is among the strongest means of removing bodily attachments that veil divine light from human spirits; people of spiritual unveiling reach that light only through fasting.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet is quoted saying that if satans did not hover around human hearts, people would see the kingdom of the heavens; no grading is stated.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The shared spiritual character of fasting and Quran revelation explains why the month that receives revelation is specifically assigned fasting.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفراء والأخفش | reports | Al-Farra and al-Akhfash take the nominative as predicate of an omitted subject, replacing 'days': the counted days are the month of Ramadan.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو علي | reports | Abu Ali allows shahr in the nominative as a subject with an omitted predicate: among the fasts prescribed is the fast of Ramadan.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Some grammarians allow shahr as a subject whose predicate is the relative clause, 'in which the Quran was revealed.'
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو علي | prefers | Abu Ali prefers taking the relative clause as an adjective of shahr, which makes the command to fast the month explicit; using it as the predicate would only state that Quran was revealed then.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | In the accusative, one analysis supplies an imperative: 'Fast the month of Ramadan.'
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second accusative analysis makes shahr a substitute for the counted days.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshaf proposes that the accusative shahr is the object of 'that you fast.'
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection to al-Kashshaf's parsing is that it separates the subject from its predicate with the long clause 'in which Quran was revealed ... is better,' an impermissible break between what functions as one unit.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Shahr derives from visibility or fame: the month is named for its clear appearance, and people need to know it to time debts, rites, fasting, and pilgrimage.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | If Ramadan is God's name, the month shares it because sins disappear in God's mercy, or because they burn through the month's blessing.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Some say the month is named after the crescent because it is conspicuous and clear.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says Ramadan is one of God's names, so 'the month of Ramadan' means the month of God.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from the Prophet says not to say Ramadan came or went, but to say the month of Ramadan, because Ramadan is one of God's names; no grading is given.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil derives Ramadan from ramda', a pre-autumn rain that washes dust from the earth; by analogy, the month washes the community's bodies of sins and purifies hearts.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Another derivation is ramad, the heat of sun-scorched stones: the name evokes burning hunger and severe hardship; it was also called tabi' because it followed and distressed people.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A further explanation says the transferred month names were given from the seasons in which they fell, and Ramadan coincided with days of intense heat.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from the Prophet explains Ramadan as the month that burns God's servants' sins; no grading is stated.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p71/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأزهري | reports | Al-Azhari derives Ramadan from the verb for tempering a blade between stones until thin; weapons were tempered during this month for use.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p72/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from the Prophet dates Abraham's scrolls to Ramadan's first night, the Torah to its sixth, the Gospel to its thirteenth, and the Quran to its twenty-fourth; no grading is stated.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p72/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi raises the problem that the Quran came to Muhammad piecemeal over twenty-three years, with portions revealed in months other than Ramadan, so the verse needs explanation.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p72/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The first answer is that the entire Quran descended on Laylat al-Qadr to the lowest heaven, then came down to earth gradually; this arrangement may have benefited the angels, the Prophet, or Gabriel.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p72/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi refers to his explanation of why revelation was gradual at Quran 25:32, where disbelievers ask why it was not sent all at once. | mentions 25:32
[RAZI-FULL:v5p72/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · محمد بن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Ishaq's second answer is that revelation began on Laylat al-Qadr in Ramadan; beginnings of religions and states mark history because they are noble and occur at known, fixed times.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:185#12/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | Hanafis require fasting from anyone who enters Ramadan legally competent, neither insane nor unconscious.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:185#12/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | A person insane throughout Ramadan owes no make-up because he did not witness the month in a state that obligates fasting.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:185#14/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | A Shawwal crescent seen in daylight on Ramadan’s thirtieth day belongs to the coming night, so it does not end that day’s fast.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:185#14/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · علي وابن مسعود وابن عمر وأنس بن مالك ومالك والشافعي وأبو حنيفة ومحمد بن الحسن والليث والأوزاعي وأحمد وإسحق | reports | Abu Umar attributes the same position to Ali, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Umar, Anas, and the listed jurists: the daytime crescent is for the next night.

[NASAFI-FULL:v1p90/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Ramadan derives from رمض, burning from hot ground; it became the month’s name and is indeclinable because it is definite and ends in ألف ونون. The name recalls hunger’s hardship or seasonal heat.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p90/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | In the hadith صام رمضان, شهر is omitted from شهر رمضان; the omission is understood from context and causes no ambiguity.

[NASAFI-FULL:v1p90/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Anyone present and resident during the month must fast it; a traveler need not fast while traveling.

[QASHANI:2:185/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Ramadan signifies the soul burning in the light of the Real.
[QASHANI:2:185/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The Quran is comprehensive, undifferentiated knowledge, the Quranic intellect leading to unity and guiding humanity through comprehensiveness.
[QASHANI:2:185/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The clear signs are proofs of union and distinction: detailed knowledge called the discriminative or Furqanic intellect.
[QASHANI:2:185/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Witnessing the month means reaching the station of witnessing the Essence; fasting means refraining from speech, act, or movement not in God.
[QASHANI:2:185/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The sick have heart diseases caused by psychic veils; travelers are still journeying and must traverse further stations before essential witnessing.
[QASHANI:2:185/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Ease is arrival at unity and extension through God's power; hardship is forcing deeds through the weak, incapable self.
[QASHANI:2:185/r7] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Completing the count means completing successive stations, states, and ranks that lead to the goal.
[QASHANI:2:185/r8] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Magnifying God means recognizing His greatness for guiding you to unity; gratitude is steadfastness in His command.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p172/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The month is a time span marked by the moon's first concealment through its disappearance and renewed appearance; it is named for its public visibility and people's need for it.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p188/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · معاذ بن جبل وابن عمر وسلمة بن الأكوع والحسن البصري والشعبي وعكرمة وابن شهاب والضحاك | reports | Most exegetes say residents able to fast were initially free to fast or feed a poor person, then that option was abrogated by the command to fast when Ramadan is present.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p192#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | On that parsing, فمن شهد منكم الشهر is the predicate; the author rejects treating its فاء as extra or comparing it with the relative clause after unrestricted الموت, since this شهر is definite and the clause has a verbal antecedent.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p193/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisa'i parses شهر رمضان as an appositive to الصيام; the author objects to the distant separation and says it reverses the usual content relation of apposition of inclusion.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p195#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | He prefers explaining Ibn Kathir’s reading of al-Qurʾān as transferring the hamza vowel to the rāʾ and dropping the hamza throughout the Qurʾān.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p195#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Al-furqān conveys that clear signs distinguish truth from falsehood, and its sound also echoes the preceding verse-endings, making it apt in meaning and cadence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p195/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil says the Qur'an descended from the Preserved Tablet to the heavenly scribes in the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree, and Gabriel brought it down over twenty years.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p201/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He says Ibn ʿAṭiyya mislabels the analysis as Basran: treating the lām as the direct-object lām conflicts with also making it part of an elided-an construction.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p201/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya proposes that the lām is a command lām and the wāw coordinates one independent clause with another.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The definite article in al-ʿidda most likely refers to make-up days missed in illness or travel, so one fasts an equal number of days later.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن القاسم وعلي بن زياد | reports | They distinguish departure before versus after sunrise: an early departure waits until sunrise, while a later one includes takbīr en route and while waiting for the imam.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أحمد | reports | Reports from Aḥmad differ on when takbīr stops at the prayer ground; Abū Yaʿlā reads one report as ending when the imam appears, while Ḥanbal says it ends after the sermon.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك، الشافعي، أحمد، أبو يوسف، محمد | reports | Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Abū Yūsuf, and Muḥammad treat Eid al-Aḍḥā and Eid al-Fiṭr alike for takbīr; Abū Ḥanīfa restricts it to Aḍḥā.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority say the formula is Allahu akbar three times, a form transmitted from Jābir; other formulas add tahlīl, tasbīḥ, or praise.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن المبارك | reports | Ibn al-Mubārak’s formula adds the testimony of God’s oneness, praise, and gratitude for guidance.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-ʿArabī says his school chose unrestricted takbīr, which he considers the appa

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | An alternative takes the count to mean a complete lunar Ramadan, whether it has twenty-nine or thirty days.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The lām in “that you magnify God” is coordinated with the lām in completing the count and has the same grammatical analysis.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Takbīr here means magnifying and praising God in any words of praise, not necessarily the formula Allahu akbar.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Others take the phrase as the specific takbīr at sighting the Shawwāl crescent; Ibn ʿAbbās says Muslims must magnify God when they see it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · سفيان | reports | Sufyān identifies the takbīr with the Eid al-Fiṭr day.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says takbīr begins at the crescent and lasts until the sermon ends, pausing when the imam goes out and resuming with him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī’s reported period runs from sighting the crescent until the imam goes out to prayer.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · زيد بن أسلم ومالك | reports | Zayd b. Aslam and Mālik begin takbīr when a person leaves home and continue until the imam goes out.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He rejects the command-lām analysis: the second-person imperative with an overt address prefix and lām is a rare poor dialect, and no reader is reported to have made this lām vowelless.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Since command lām would be read with the other command-lām forms, the reported reading supports a prepositional, not imperative, lām; the wāw then coordinates phrases rather than clauses.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī makes the lām causal and coordinates it with an omitted cause: God wills ease so that people complete the count.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ supplies an omitted verb after the wāw: the act was done so that the count would be completed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj makes it coordinated with an omitted cause whose result is also omitted: God did this to ease matters and to complete the count.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a Kūfan view that places the implied causal act after its purpose: the concession was granted so you could complete the count.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قائلون | reports | Another proposal treats the wāw as extra, yielding “God wills ease in order to complete the count”; Abū Ḥayyān calls it weak.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī assigns the implied act “He legislated this” to the whole passage: completing the count, magnifying God, and giving thanks each have a distinct purpose.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p202/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | He calls this distribution of purposes a subtle rhetorical “folding” construction that only expert critics readily unpack.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المنتخب | prefers | Al-Muntakhab prefers taking completion of the count as Ramadan fasting and magnification as takbīr at its end for guidance to obedience, not generic glorification.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المنتخب | reports | It argues that general glorification is already required at all times and in every act of worship, so it would not be specially mentioned here.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The preposition ʿalā attached to takabbirū carries a causal implication, as in thanking someone for a favor.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī explains the elevated preposition as takbīr carrying an implied sense of praise: magnify God while praising Him for guiding you.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He says al-Zamakhsharī’s wording explains the meaning, not the syntax; syntactically the sense is to praise God through takbīr for His guidance.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The apparent reading makes mā a verbal noun, meaning “for your being guided”; reading it as “that which” requires two unlikely omissions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | If mā is relative, the phrase means guidance to the Islamic law, or guidance away from the Christians’ alteration of fasting.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes “perhaps you will give thanks” as human-oriented hope and thanks for guidance.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p203/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation makes the thanks due for the reward God grants for acts of obedience.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p204/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari interprets “so that you may give thanks” as God’s intention, construing divine hope as will.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p204/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya assigns the hope to human beings, since literal hoping is impossible for God.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p204/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | He regards the two analyses as comparable and observes that hard duties such as fasting and retaliation end with hope of piety, while concessions such as breaking the fast end with hope of gratitude. | mentions 2:183, 2:179
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Legal obligations characteristically begin with what is easier and proceed to the required limit, where the ruling settles.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The month’s virtue is tied to revelation of the Qur’an; residents must fast it, while the sick and traveler make up what they missed after recovery or settling, in keeping with divine intent to ease the burden.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p228/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The prescribed month, exemption for illness and travel, and divine desire for ease serve completion of the count, magnification of God, and gratitude, each law being paired with its fitting purpose.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#10/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | على ما هداكم is governed by تكبروا. على retains its ordinary sense of elevation because تكبير incorporates the sense of praising God.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#10/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | rejects | Al-Zamakhsharī paraphrases this as magnifying God while praising Him; the Shaykh says this explains meaning, not syntax, since على would then modify the implied حامدين.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#10/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The alternative takes على as لام التعليل; the author prefers its ordinary sense because figurative use of a preposition is weak.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#10/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | ما is most clearly a verbal noun, meaning His guidance of you; the alternative makes it a relative pronoun and needs an omitted object pronoun and an omitted noun such as following.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#10/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | rejects | The relative-pronoun parse is remote: it deletes the object هداكموه and needs an omitted noun to yield the sense following what guided you.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#10/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The verse closes with hope of gratitude because it follows ease and legal concession; the preceding difficult duties end with hope of piety. The pattern is concessions followed by thanks, unreduced burdens by piety. | mentions 2:179, 2:178
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The less common reading puts شهر رمضان in the accusative.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ذو الرمة | reports | Dhu al-Rumma's line sees the thin crescent before other people, witnessing شهر as the visible moon.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفراء والثعلبي | reports | The moon's name extended to the period beginning with its rising: رأيت الشهر means its crescent; Farra reports أشهرنا and al-Tha'labi says شهر الهلال means it rose.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The regular plural is أشهر for a small number and شهور for many.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The best accusative parse supplies an imperative: صوموا شهر رمضان.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأخفش والرماني | reports | Al-Akhfash and al-Rummani parse شهر as بدل from أياما معدودات, supporting the view that the numbered days are Ramadan, though the author notes the separation.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو عبيدة والحوفي | reports | Abu Ubayda and al-Hawfi parse the accusative as نصب على الإغراء.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية والزمخشري | rejects | Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari link the accusative to وأن تصوموا, but the author rejects splitting the relative clause across unrelated خير; شهر is a direct object, not an adverb.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A fifth parse makes شهر the object of تعملون after deleting an إضافة: تعلمون شرف شهر رمضان.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو عمر | holds | Abu Amr assimilates the راء of شهر into the راء of رمضان; the author rejects Ibn Atiyya's objection because reliable transmission prevails over analogy.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The common definition of شهر is a period from the new moon's initial concealment until it disappears; its name reflects people's nee

[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#2/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says شهر names the moon itself, called so for its visibility; a cited saying compares it to a fingernail clipping.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ramadan is the generic proper name for this specific month.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The hamzated word derives from قرأ, 'to gather', because the Quran gathers suras, verses, rulings, and admonitions.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن كثير | holds | Ibn Kathir reads القرآن without hamza; the author gives two derivations for this form.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The more evident analysis is نقل: like Warsh, Ibn Kathir transfers the hamza vowel to the preceding consonant and deletes it, a special choice due to frequent use and combining two forms. | mentions 23:1
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r13] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The alternative derives it from قرنت, 'joined two things', on pattern فعال because the Quran joins its suras, verses, rulings, and admonitions.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r14] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Derivation from قريت الماء في الحوض ('collected water in a basin') is wrong because the two roots are distinct.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r15] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | In أنزل فيه القرآن, القرآن is نائب الفاعل.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r16] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | أنزل فيه القرآن may mean revelation occurred in Ramadan, some specifying its twenty-fourth day; another view takes فيه as concerning Ramadan's status and merit.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One etymology says Ramadan arrived during the intense summer heat الرمضاء, like Rabi and Jumada named for their seasons.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Other proposed derivations say Ramadan burns sins away and hearts burn from admonition.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A blade etymology describes thinning a blade between stones; a sharpened blade is called رميض or مرموض.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · المفضل | reports | The month was called ناتق in pre-Islamic times; al-Mufaddal's poem uses that name.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari derives رمضان as a verbal noun from رمض إذا احترق; the author says this requires attestation because فعَلان is not usually a verbal noun of an intransitive verb.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Another etymology connects the name to pre-autumn rain that cleans dust from earth, analogously cleansing hearts of sins.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | القرآن was originally the verbal noun of قرأت and later became the name for what lies between the covers.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#3/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · حسان | reports | Hassan's verse about Uthman uses قرآنا as a verbal noun, evidence for القرآن's original مصدر meaning.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | هدى is an accusative حال from القرآن, governed by أنزل; as a مصدر it may mean ذو هدى, function as هاديا, or intensively be guidance itself.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | للناس either attaches to هدى if it means هاد, or is an omitted phrase adjectivally qualifying the preceding indefinite noun.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | هدى cannot predicate omitted هو because بينات is overtly accusative; بينات is a second necessary حال and a specific kind of general guidance, which includes hidden and manifest matters.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | من الهدى والفرقان qualifies هدى وبينات in the accusative and depends on an omitted phrase: the Quran's guidance and proofs are part of God's guidance and proofs.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | الفرقان replaces البينات because it adds the sense of distinguishing truth from falsehood and echoes the preceding verse endings.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | Some say the first هدى denotes the foundations of religion and the second its branches.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya treats the second الهدى as anaphoric to the first, citing the definite repetition pattern, Pharaoh's messenger, and Ibn Abbas's saying about one hardship and two eases. | mentions 73:15, 73:16
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author rejects Ibn Atiyya's anaphoric reading: since هدى and بينات are حال, من الهدى cannot modify either or both without circularly qualifying the Quran by a part identical to the whole.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | من الهدى cannot attach to بينات as a qualifier either: replacing الهدى by منه is invalid; the author therefore takes الهدى and الفرقان generally, with هدى وبينات a subset.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · السلمي وأبو حيوة | reports | Al-Sulami, Abu Haywa, and others preserve the original kasra of the imperative لام throughout the Quran.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفراء | reports | Farra reports that opening the imperative لام is a Sulaym dialect; some restrict it to cases where the following ya is open.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | من in فمن شهد may be relative or conditional; the conditional parse is more apparent.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | منكم is a حال of the implicit subject of شهد, governed by an omitted كائنا.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa calls منكم a حال of the subject and also attaches it to شهد; the author calls that contradictory, but allows semantic attachment through كائنا.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One parse makes الشهر an adverb: شهد means 'was present', with an omitted object such as the city.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The preferred direct-object parse estimates دخول الشهر; هلال الشهر is weak because Arabic says شاهدت الهلال, and it would wrongly require everyone seeing the crescent to fast.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari parses الشهر and the pronoun in فليصمه as adverbs because residents and travelers both witness the month; the author objects that verbs do not govern adverb pronouns without في unless broadened to object-case.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | فاء may mark the conditional answer or be extra in a predicate after relative من; the لام is imperative.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#6/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الجمهور | holds | The majority read the imperative لام with sukun, analogizing its position after واو or فاء to the connected form كتف.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#7/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The definite article in الشهر is anaphoric; a pronoun could replace it, but the noun is expressed overtly to honor the month.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The author refers the meaning and derivation of يريد to his discussion at 2:26. | mentions 2:26
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | اراد usually takes concrete objects with باء and verbal nouns directly, though the pattern can reverse; the poetic witness has أرادت عرارا بالهوان.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#7/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa reads باء as attachment: God figuratively attaches ease to you through allowing breaking the fast when excused.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa calls the denial of hardship emphatic, since saying God wills ease would suffice.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#7/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو جعفر ويحيى بن وثاب وابن هرمز | reports | Abu Ja'far, Yahya ibn Waththab, and Ibn Hurmuz read yusr and ʿusr with damma on sīn; grammarians differ on original damma versus assimilation, and the author prefers damma as customary.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#8/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية والزمخشري وأبو البقاء | reports | One view makes لام extra before implied أن, with ولتكملوا coordinated to اليسر as object; the long separation weakens the verb's governance, so لام restores it.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#8/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو صخر | reports | Abu Sakhr's أريد لأنسى حبها illustrates the extra لام construction.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#8/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra takes the لام as causal and supplies a deleted verb after واو: ولتكملوا العدة فعل هذا.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:185#8/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj coordinates it with an omitted cause and omits its consequence: فعل الله ذلك ليسهل عليكم ولتكملوا.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p501/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God praises Ramadan above the other months because He chose it for the descent of the great Qur’an; revelation of earlier divine books also occurred in this month.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p501/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report transmitted by Ahmad says Abraham’s scrolls came down on Ramadan’s first night, the Torah on its sixth, the Gospel on its thirteenth, and the Qur’an on its twenty-fourth.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p501/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جابر بن عبد الله | reports | Ibn Mardawayh transmits from Jabir that the Zabur descended on Ramadan’s twelfth night and the Gospel on its eighteenth, with the remaining dates as in the preceding report.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p501/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The earlier scriptures each descended all at once to their respective prophets, whereas the Qur’an first descended whole to Bayt al-ʿIzza in the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr, then piecemeal to Muhammad according to events.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p501/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Replying to ʿAtiyya al-Aswad’s concern that revelation occurred in other months, Ibn ʿAbbas said the Qur’an descended whole in Ramadan on the blessed Night of Decree, then gradually across months and days. | mentions 97:1, 44:3
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p502#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The Qur’an guides the hearts of those who believe, affirm, and follow it; its clear proofs are understood by reflection, validate its guidance, oppose error, and distinguish truth from falsehood and lawful from unlawful.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p502#2/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · البخاري | reports | Al-Bukhari supports using “Ramadan” alone by titling a chapter “It is said Ramadan” and citing reports such as the promise that fasting Ramadan with faith and seeking reward brings forgiveness.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p502/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | In Saʿid ibn Jubayr’s report, Ibn ʿAbbas says the Qur’an descended to the lowest heaven and Bayt al-ʿIzza midway through Ramadan, then came to the Prophet over twenty years in response to people’s words.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p502/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | In ʿIkrima’s report, Ibn ʿAbbas says the Qur’an descended whole to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr; God then supplied the Prophet’s responses whenever the polytheists raised an argument. | mentions 25:32, 25:33

[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Shahr Ramadan is a subject whose predicate follows; the sentence highlights the month’s virtue and explains why its fast was prescribed.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Qur’an was sent as guidance for people to the straight path, through its inimitability and other features.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Qur’an also contains clear signs guiding to truth and distinguishing it from falsehood through its wisdom and rulings; guidance has more than one category.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The fast of Ramadan is obligatory for whoever witnesses the month, as stated in the verse’s following command.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Arabic word for month is shahr because the month is widely known; Ramadan is a verbal noun from ramida, to burn, and the compound is a proper name made diptote by its ending.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Ramadan may be named for livers burning from hunger and thirst, sins burning away through fasting, or the month’s occurrence during intense heat.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | One account says month names were borrowed from an older language and assigned according to the season at naming, as with Ramadan’s hot days, spring, and frozen water in Jumada.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | An alternative view holds that Ramadan is one of God’s names; a Prophetic report therefore advises saying “the month of Ramadan,” not “Ramadan came” or “Ramadan went.”
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Qur’an first descended to Bayt al-ʿIzza in the lowest heaven, then Gabriel brought it down in portions over twenty-three years according to divine will.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي | reports | A Prophetic report dates the Scrolls of Abraham to Ramadan’s first night, the Torah to its sixth day, the Gospel to its thirteenth, and the Qur’an to its twenty-fourth.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Qur’an derives from qarʾ, gathering, because it brings together the knowledge of earlier and later people.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verse first names guidance as a genus, then singles out its clear kinds; this honorific coordination intensifies the description through three levels, and the clear mode is the superior division.
[BURSEVI:v1p238#3/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God intends ease by permitting breaking the fast during travel or illness; yusr means what is made easy.
